summary:
I've been building Keikochō, a Japanese-learning app for myself, and lately most of the interesting work has been in getting the details right rather than adding features. The grammar section had a real gap I only found by measuring it: primer lengths ranged from 84 words to 504 words depending on when I'd written them, and nobody had gone back to level up the early ones. Fixed it by splitting each grammar point into a short primer for the drill screen and a separate study-guide block for the reference pages — one authored file, two jobs, so they can't drift out of sync with each other.

The other recurring theme is that plausible output is the dangerous kind, not broken output. A CSS grid I used for a two-column list quietly split a sentence's inline markup across grid cells, so half of it landed in a 13px marker column — nothing errored, and it read exactly like intentional vertical Japanese until I actually measured the row heights and found one row was 30x taller than its neighbors. Same lesson on the audio side: a text-to-speech pipeline mispronounced a handful of words, and the fix wasn't to patch around the bad output — it was to treat the mispronunciation as a signal about the input text and fix the word list upstream.

On the infrastructure side, I run local models on a couple of GPUs and had a nasty one this summer: a speech-recognition service that returned healthy status codes while every actual transcription failed with an out-of-memory error. Turned out two services shared a GPU, one auto-sized its memory allocation at boot and the other loaded lazily on first request — so whichever one started first on any given reboot won the race, and the loser broke intermittently in a way that looked like a network bug. Pinning the allocation instead of letting it auto-size fixed it for good; a "verified working" reading on a shared GPU is really just one sample from a distribution.

highlights.oneLiner: GPU broker for local models; chased a boot-order VRAM race between two co-resident services
Pinned auto-sizing VRAM allocation after a shared-GPU race caused intermittent OOM failures
